title: Îles Flottantes
subtitle: Floating islands of poached meringue on vanilla crème anglaise
excerpt: Soft poached meringue domes floating on a pool of vanilla custard, finished with threads of caramel. The name means 'floating islands', the white meringue islands sit on a golden crème anglaise sea.
sourceNotes: Îles flottantes is a classical French dessert appearing in Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903). The dish uses both parts of the egg: yolks go into the crème anglaise, whites are whipped and poached into the meringue islands. Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), gives the recipe. Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961), gives the full method with detailed crème anglaise instructions. The dish is sometimes confused with œufs à la neige (snow eggs), a very similar preparation.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The crème anglaise can be made up to 2 days ahead and kept refrigerated. Poach the meringue and make the caramel within 1 hour of serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A pourable English-style vanilla custard sauce made from egg yolks, sugar, and milk. The custard must be cooked very gently — it thickens at around 82°C and will curdle and scramble above that temperature. A properly made crème anglaise coats the back of a spoon and leaves a clear line when a finger is drawn through it.

content.text: Îles flottantes is a two-component dessert: soft meringue poached in sweetened milk, and
made from the yolks of the same eggs. Both can be made ahead. The caramel is the final flourish, poured over the meringue immediately before serving so it sets into crisp amber threads.

items.prepNote: separated: yolks for the custard, whites for the meringue
divided: 60 g for the custard, 40 g for the meringue

content.text: Warm the milk in a saucepan with the vanilla until steaming. Whisk the 4 egg yolks with 60 g sugar in a bowl until pale. Pour the hot milk onto the yolks in a slow stream, whisking constantly.

Return to the saucepan over medium-low heat. Stir constantly with a wooden spoon, scraping the base and sides, until the custard thickens enough to coat the back of the spoon and hold a clear line when your finger is drawn through it (about 82°C). Do not boil.
Strain through the fine sieve into a clean jug. Cool, then refrigerate.
Whisk the 4 egg whites to stiff peaks with the electric mixer. Add 40 g sugar and whisk until glossy and firm.

Half-fill a wide shallow pan with water and bring to a barely-trembling simmer. Using two large spoons or an ice cream scoop, shape the meringue into 8 domed ovals and lower into the water. Poach for 2 minutes, flip gently, poach for 2 minutes more. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper.

Pour the cold crème anglaise into shallow bowls. Float 2 meringue islands in each bowl. For the caramel: heat 80 g sugar in a dry saucepan over medium heat, swirling gently, until it turns a deep amber. Remove from the heat immediately. Working quickly, use a spoon to drizzle threads of hot caramel over the meringues. It will set in seconds. Serve immediately.

items.cause: The custard was allowed to boil, or the heat was too high.
items.fix: Remove from the heat immediately and plunge the base of the pan into cold water. Whisk vigorously and strain. If it has curdled badly, blend briefly with a hand blender and strain, this can rescue a slightly scrambled custard if the damage is not too severe.

items.symptom: The meringue islands have collapsed and become dense
items.cause: The water was at a full boil rather than a barely-trembling simmer.
items.fix: The poaching water must be just below simmering, not bubbling at all. Rolling boiling water tears the meringue apart. A very gentle simmer (79 to 82°C) gives firm, puffy islands.

Work very fast once the caramel is made, it cools and sets in 20 to 30 seconds off the heat. If it solidifies in the pan, return to low heat briefly to reliquefy. Have everything else assembled and ready before starting the caramel.

content.text: Îles flottantes belongs to the French tradition of egg-based desserts. Both parts of the egg are used: the yolks go into the custard, the whites become the meringue. The dish appears in the classical French repertoire as an elegant, light dessert suitable for the end of a formal dinner. It requires technique rather than expensive ingredients, which made it a favourite in professional kitchens where skill mattered more than budget.
